one_liner: Research secure malloc (CCS 2017) with near-glibc speed, far faster than the DieHarder and OpenBSD secure allocators.
what_it_does: FreeGuard is an LD_PRELOAD (or link-time) replacement for malloc, free, calloc, realloc, memalign and posix_memalign on Linux that adds heap-overflow, use-after-free, double-free and invalid-free defences. It also interposes pthread_create to put every thread on its own fixed 8 MB stack slot. No source changes are needed, but it is built with its own Makefile into libfreeguard.so.
how_it_is_fast: It is a BiBOP (big bag of pages) allocator: power-of-two size classes, per-thread heaps, bump-pointer allocation and per-bag freelists kept in separate shadow memory, so most allocations take no lock and need no in-object headers. The thread index comes from shifting the stack address (each thread runs in a fixed 8 MB stack slot), not from a TLS lookup. Security is added cheaply on top: four randomly chosen bag sets per size class, randomised 4-16 MB bag sizes, a 10% chance of a guard page at each page boundary, a one-byte canary per object checked on free together with two neighbours each side, and FIFO freelists that delay reuse.
when_to_use: Research or hardening experiments that need overflow, double-free and use-after-free mitigation on multithreaded Linux x86-64 programs at about glibc speed (1.8% average overhead in the paper, per search snippets).
Replacing DieHarder or OpenBSD-style malloc where their 22-36% (geometric mean) slowdown is unacceptable.
Programs with at most a few dozen threads, ordinary malloc/free/realloc use and no over-aligned allocations.
As a readable reference design for a BiBOP secure allocator with shadow-memory metadata (the same group's successor is Guarder).
when_not_to_use: When raw speed is the goal: it is at best about glibc speed, and canneal and freqmine exceeded 10% overhead in the paper (per search snippets).
C++17 code that uses over-aligned new, or any code calling aligned_alloc, valloc or pvalloc: FreeGuard's versions print an error and return NULL, and malloc_usable_size is not provided.
Programs with more than 128 live threads, threads that need stacks larger than about 8 MB, or code that runs on fibers, coroutine stacks or sigaltstack handlers (see gotchas).

Production use: abandoned since January 2018, a reported malloc(SIZE_MAX) integer overflow still in the source, random seed taken from time(NULL), and invalid frees of non-heap pointers only logged (open issues #2 and #3).

Memory-constrained deployments: power-of-two classes plus the canary byte round a 16-byte request up to a 32-byte block, and startup reserves terabytes of virtual address space (MAP_NORESERVE), which fails under ulimit -v.

integration.dependencies: libdl, libpthread, librt; bundled SSE2 random-number generator (rng/sse2rng.c)
integration.min_toolchain: C++11; the Makefile uses clang++ -O2 with a hard-coded GCC 4.8 libstdc++ include path (the paper reportedly used GCC 4.9.1, unverified)
integration.platforms: Linux x86-64 only (glibc __libc_start_main and pthread interposition, -msse2, x86 inline assembly)
integration.thread_safety: Thread-safe through per-thread heaps plus per-bag spinlocks on freelists; at most 128 live threads, and threads are only recognised if created through the interposed pthread_create.
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — LD_PRELOAD covers malloc, free, calloc, realloc, memalign and posix_memalign, but aligned_alloc, valloc and pvalloc return NULL, malloc_usable_size is missing, every thread stack is forced to 8 MB minus guard pages, and memory overhead is higher than glibc.

gotchas: Security bugs in the shipped source: the canary byte is added to the size with no overflow check, so malloc(SIZE_MAX) returns a small valid block (issue #1, closed in 2021, though no commit has landed since 2018); calloc multiplies nelem by elsize without an overflow check; srand is seeded with time(NULL) (issue #2, 'Guessable random').

xthread::thread_create has no return statement, so the interposed pthread_create returns an indeterminate value (undefined behaviour; -Wall warns). When all 128 thread slots are in use, allocThreadIndex hands back an out-of-range index with no check. Source reading, not tested.

The thread index is computed from the current stack address; code running outside FreeGuard's stack slots (fibers, ucontext or Boost.Context stacks, sigaltstack handlers) maps to thread 0 and shares its unlocked bump pointer with the main thread. Source reading, not tested.

The README says plain make uses rand(), but the Makefile always defines SSE2RNG and MANYBAGS, and the security features (guard pages, random guards, canaries, FIFO freelist) are on unless NO_SECURITY is set; destroy-on-free is off by default, unlike the DieHarder configuration it was compared with.
pick_this_over_siblings_when: None of the speed-oriented siblings (mimalloc, jemalloc, snmalloc, TCMalloc) is described in this catalog as a secure allocator with randomised layout, guard pages and canaries, so FreeGuard is the pick only when those defences matter more than speed; for throughput over glibc, choose mimalloc or snmalloc, and NUMAlloc from the same UTSA group for NUMA machines.
verified_claims_summary: Per WebSearch snippets of the CCS 2017 paper (the paper itself could not be opened): over 19 multithreaded applications (11 PARSEC plus Apache, Firefox, MySQL, Memcached, SQLite and others), averaged over ten runs and normalised to the default glibc allocator, FreeGuard ran 1.8% slower (arithmetic mean; 1.4% geometric), OpenBSD malloc 34% (22% geometric) and DieHarder 88% (36% geometric). Hardware, compiler and memory-overhead figures were not confirmed, and the repository carries no benchmark code.
status_note: Abandoned since 2018-01-04 (6 commits, no releases, issues #2 and #3 open without replies); GPL-2.0 with a paid commercial licence from UTSA, so copying it into proprietary code needs that licence; the group's successor is Guarder.
sources_read: WebSearch snippets of https://arxiv.org/pdf/1709.02746 (page not opened)
